articles.title: The Third Cup: After Everything Has a Name
articles.description: Names didn't create the world. They connected us to it.     It was three in the afternoon. The café...
articles.body_html:
Names didn't create the world. They connected us to it.

It was three in the afternoon. The café was quiet.

A customer was sitting by the window, his laptop open. He stared at the screen, typed a few lines, deleted them, then started again. He had been at it for quite a while.

I brought his coffee over.

"Code giving you trouble today?"

"The code is fine. I'm the one who's not happy."

"What's wrong?"

"Variable naming. This one's called data, that one's also called data, and another one is called result. I can understand them now, but when I come back in a few months, I'll probably have to do some archaeology on my own code."

I laughed.

"At least you remember writing it."

"Last week I found a variable called final_result_new_v2."

"Then there must be another one called final_result_new_v2_really_final."

He looked up at me.

"Have you been secretly reading our company's codebase?"

"No need. I can guess."

He took a sip of coffee, then picked up the menu on the table.

"By the way, there's something I've been meaning to ask you."

"What is it?"

He pointed at the menu.

"Why do all six coffees on your menu have a person's name beside them?"

I glanced at it.

"You mean those names?"

"Yes. The pour-over says Mark, the espresso says P, and there are a few others. Are those the baristas' names, or did they come up with the recipes themselves?"

"Neither. Each one belongs to one of my regulars."

He looked up.

"You actually name coffees after your customers?"

"More or less. Each of them has their own usual coffee. When they come in, I know what to make."

He looked at the menu again.

"So they don't even have to order?"

"After a while, I don't even need to ask what they want."

He laughed.

"Your café's naming system is more complicated than our variable naming."

I looked at the six coffees on the menu, each with a regular's name beside it.

"Actually, names are more interesting than people think."

I walked over to the bookshelf and took down an old copy of the Tao Te Ching.

"Speaking of names, that reminds me of something Laozi wrote."

I opened the book to Chapter 42 and placed it in front of him.

"The Dao gives birth to One. One gives birth to Two. Two gives birth to Three. Three gives birth to the ten thousand things."

He read it once.

"Can that solve my variable naming problem?"

"I can't promise it'll fix your bugs, but we can talk about it."

"Go ahead. The code isn't going anywhere."

From One to Two

I drew one solid line and one broken line on a paper napkin.

"In my understanding, the One here is the Dao, and the Two are Yin and Yang."

"I know Yin and Yang. That black-and-white fish symbol, right?"

"That's the one. Light and darkness, movement and stillness, above and below, cold and heat. They're different, but they depend on each other and keep changing in relation to each other."

He looked at the two lines.

"So, one is 1 and the other is 0?"

"We can use binary as a modern analogy, but they're not exactly the same thing. Yin and Yang aren't just two fixed states. The relationship between them matters too."

He nodded.

"Got it. You're explaining ancient philosophy through modern IT."

"Just finding a familiar way in. Don't go around telling people Laozi was a programmer who never open-sourced his code."

He laughed.

"Maybe he just kept the repository private."

So, What Is the Three?

I drew a little human figure beside the two lines.

"Now, the Three is where I have my own interpretation."

He looked at the napkin.

"Wait. Does the original text actually mention human beings?"

"No. This is my own reading. Laozi doesn't spell it out that way."

"So you're adding a new requirement to Laozi's spec?"

I laughed.

"Do programmers always want to submit a change request when they hear something new?"

I continued.

"To me, the Three is the human being alongside Yin and Yang. Yin and Yang were already part of the world. When human beings appeared, we started observing things, telling them apart, and giving them names."

"But everything already existed before humans showed up, didn't it?"

"Of course. Mountains, rivers, trees, birds and animals didn't wait for us to appear."

I pointed out the window.

"That mountain was already there. The river was flowing. The trees were growing. We didn't create any of them. We just started giving them names."

He thought about it for a moment.

"So the names let us recognize things, remember them, and talk about them with other people?"

"Exactly. Without names, how would you tell me which mountain you climbed or which tree you saw on your way here?"

He nodded.

I wrote a sentence on the napkin:

The world existed long before us. Through naming, we found a way to connect with it.

He glanced at it.

"That's pretty good. Better than any of my variable names."

"Your variable names aren't beyond saving."

Six Coffees, Six Names

Speaking of naming, I looked toward the menu beside the counter.

"Those six coffees you asked about are another example."

He turned around.

"How so?"

"Well, they started out as six different coffees. Then six people kept coming back, each with their own favorite. After a while, I started putting their names beside those drinks on the menu. Mark has the pour-over. P has the espresso. The others have their own favorites too."

"What if Mark wants an espresso one day?"

"Of course he can have one. It's a menu, not a life sentence."

He laughed.

"I thought you were going to make him drink pour-over for the rest of his life."

"That would be a quick way to put this café out of business."

We both laughed.

I glanced at the menu again.

"Now, when I see those names, I think of the people behind them. Sometimes I remember a conversation, an argument, or something that happened here. A few names can bring back quite a lot."

He looked at the menu.

"So the coffee comes with a memory?"

"Something like that. The coffee is still coffee. But those names mean a little more to me now."

He nodded.

"Kind of like variables in code. The value is there, and the name helps whoever comes later understand what it represents."

"Exactly. Though a name can be misleading too. Just because a field has a certain name doesn't mean it actually does what the name suggests."

"We have plenty of those in our project."

"I believe you."

Beyond Names

He closed his laptop and picked up his cup.

"Does that apply to people too? Engineer, tester, product manager... those labels don't tell you everything about someone?"

"Not even close. They tell you what someone does, but they don't tell you who that person is."

He smiled.

"So I shouldn't use job titles to label people anymore?"

"You can know what someone does. Just don't assume you've figured them out because you know their job title."

"Maybe I should give myself a new title."

"What would that be?"

"Coffee enthusiast."

I glanced at his empty cup.

"That one has some evidence behind it."

He laughed and shook his head.

I turned the napkin over.

Names help us understand the world, but they can't replace the world itself. We give things names so we can talk about them and share what we know. That doesn't mean a name tells us everything.

He looked at the Tao Te Ching on the table.

"What comes beyond names, then?"

"Plenty. Let's save that for another cup."

A Regular Walks In

The bell above the door rang.

I looked up. Mark had walked in.

He glanced at the counter, then at the Tao Te Ching on the table.

"What are you talking about today?"

"Names. And the stories behind them."

Mark didn't ask anything else. He simply walked over to his usual seat.

I didn't ask what he wanted.

I picked up the pour-over kettle, ground the beans, warmed the cup, and started pouring.

The water flowed gently over the coffee grounds, and the aroma slowly filled the space.

A little later, I placed a pour-over in front of him.

Mark looked at the coffee, then at me.

"I haven't ordered yet."

"I know."

I smiled.

"Some names don't need to be introduced every time."

He picked up the cup and took a sip.

The customer by the window looked at Mark, then back at the menu.

"So the Mark on the menu is him?"

"That's him."

"Well, now I know who's behind that coffee."

"You could say that."

He packed up his laptop and stood.

"Next time I come in, I want a spot on that menu too."​

"I already know what you like," I said. "Your name just isn't on the menu yet."

​He pointed at his empty cup.​

"Isn't that enough to start with?"

​I smiled.​

"Come back tomorrow. We'll see."

He laughed, said goodbye, and headed for the door.

Mark was still working his way through his pour-over.

I picked up the empty cups and went back behind the counter.

P.S. English isn't my first language, so I use AI to help polish my writing and smooth out the rough edges. Thanks for reading.

☕ Buy me a coffee

P.P.S. The paperback edition of my earlier book is now available.

articles.title: Crowdwide Day 33: I Tried Building Crowdwide AI... And It Went Wrong 😭
articles.description: Yo Developers!!  In the past 2–2.5 months, I worked on a social media platform called...
articles.body_html:
Yo Developers!!

In the past 2–2.5 months, I worked on a social media platform called Crowdwide.

Mainly, it's a community-building platform.

I've been learning everything, from marketing and understanding user needs to improving UI, understanding the importance of minimal UI, fixing bugs, and many other things.

After building the core things, I'm just giving it time to get established, but...

In the beginning, its growth was like 70+ visitors per day, and now it's like 5–6 visitors per day.

And the current stage is:

25 members

121 posts shared

4 communities

And for communities:

01

Crowdwide Spotlight 😎

A place where interesting users, communities, posts, projects, and creators discovered on Crowdwide get highlighted.

15 members

02

Build in Public

Share what you're building, your progress, milestones, lessons, challenges, and wins. 🚀

11 members

03

Hynaweb

Announcements and community

5 members

So, in this project, I was trying to integrate AI.

Yes... it was Crowdwide AI.

But... but... but...! So, what approach did I try?

Firstly, I tried using normal PyTorch on my local machine.

Yea, it worked pretty well.

And I tried to deploy it too, but after deployment, it started showing memory errors.

And I knew why, because I had tried to deploy that on a free plan before this too.

So, I tried to explore some better ways, and I found a way that worked.

I downloaded a free language model from Hugging Face and built a system like this:

When you ask a question, it downloads a 50–60 MB (approximately 130M parameters) file as a cache on your device, which is then used as a language model. The information from Crowdwide is given to it as context.

So, I implemented this, and it worked, but not very well. It was hallucinating a lot.

Like, that was framing some useful work and pure hallucinations!!

So, I thought maybe it needed a better model. I tried another model of 118 MB, approximately 300M parameters.

And it worked pretty well on my LOCAL MACHINE!!

So, I thought it would work there too.

I just tried to make it an agent. I gave it access to make posts, chats, polls, comments, replies in mentions, check notifications, etc. Like everything you can do... everything means EVERYTHING!!

And then I thought I should try it.

I told it to write an article on water.

That AI wrote an article on it and PUBLISHED IT, BUT ON ITS OWN!!

Like, I gave it 100% access.

So, I deleted that and made a system that would ask before publishing anything.

And now all things were working perfectly. I thought I should deploy it.

And again, the same thing happened to me. After deploying, it wasn't working well. There were memory errors, some devices were facing network issues, working with cache and running AI on the local machine was taking too much RAM, and many times it was giving errors, mainly on mobile phones.

And on computers, it was quite slow.

I thought, let's try to make it simpler.

I tried to make it so that it would be trained only on the data available on Crowdwide and would have checkpoints.

But when deployed, it gave me memory errors again.

So, I decided to remove it.

And mainly, this idea needs more critical thinking before it gets into production.

Further, I monetized Crowdwide... just like a normal publisher.

But my plan was to monetize it in such a way that communities under Crowdwide could get monetized too, and the community owner would get ad revenue!

But till now, I haven't found any way to do that.

I got the background story, but not the features.

And you'll get GTA 6 before Crowdwide features and proper monetization. 😭

This is what I tried to do, but maybe if I find a way... maybe I'll work on this again.

BTW, if you have any way to integrate this, you can suggest it. I'll definitely work on it and won't forget to mention you! lol

Links:

https://www.crowdwide.run.place/

https://github.com/DeveloperPuneet/Crowdwide

articles.title: Three hours, one small extension, and Firefox Add-ons
articles.description: After Chrome Web Store (approved in about 5 hours) and Edge Add-ons (in review), I thought Firefox...
articles.body_html:
After Chrome Web Store (approved in about 5 hours) and Edge Add-ons (in review), I thought Firefox would be the easy one. Same extension, same Manifest V3, same zip. 😅

It took me three hours. Not because the code was broken, but because Firefox Add-ons asks for a few extra things I didn't know about. Here is what I learned, so you don't have to learn it at 11 PM after a day at the factory.

1. Firefox wants an ID in the manifest

Chrome doesn't care, Firefox does:

"browser_specific_settings": {
  "gecko": {
    "id": "your-extension@yourdomain.com",
    "strict_min_version": "142.0",
    "data_collection_permissions": { "required": ["none"] }
  }
}

data_collection_permissions is now required for new extensions, and it needs Firefox 142 or newer, otherwise the validator warns you about Firefox for Android.

2. Don't delete a draft add-on

I deleted my first submission to start fresh. Big mistake: the ID and the URL slug stay reserved forever. I had to pick a new ID and a new slug. The name can stay the same, only the link changes.

3. The manifest must be at the root of the zip

If you zip the folder instead of its contents, validation fails. Open the zip: manifest.json must be the first thing you see.

4. The innerHTML warnings

The validator gave me 9 warnings: "Unsafe assignment to innerHTML". Not errors, but I wanted a clean result. So I replaced them with DOM methods:

// Before
panel.innerHTML = `<b>FPS</b> ${fps}`;

// After
const label = document.createElement("b");
label.textContent = "FPS";
panel.replaceChildren(label, ` ${fps}`);

Same HUD, same look, and the result: 0 errors, 0 warnings. ✅

The result

BeeLadybug is now waiting for review on Firefox too. Three stores, one small vanilla JS extension, and a lot of patience.

If you're publishing your first Firefox extension, I hope this saves you a few hours. And if you have a Firefox story, tell me in the comments! 🐝

articles.title: Announcing AnalogJS 3.0 ⚡️
articles.description: We're excited to announce the 3.0 release of AnalogJS! This release includes many features that help...
articles.body_html:
We're excited to announce the 3.0 release of AnalogJS! This release includes many features that help developers ship websites and full-stack applications, faster, with Angular.

Features ⭐️

Analog is the meta-framework built on top of Angular, powered by Vite, a next generation open-source build tool, and Nitro, an open-source server engine framework. Here are some of its features, including:

  • First-class support for the Vite ecosystem (Vitest, Playwright, Storybook, and more)
  • Filesystem-based routing
  • Support for markdown pages and blogs
  • Support for API/server routes
  • Hybrid SSR/SSG with sitemap and RSS feed support
  • Supports Angular CLI/Nx workspaces
  • Server and deployment support
  • And more!

What's New

Analog 3.0 contains many new features including composable Vite plugins, Nitro v2 and v3 support, type-safe routing, streaming SSR, new Angular compilation support, coding agents, and more.

Composable Vite Plugins 🔌

In previous versions, the analog() plugin set up the Angular and Nitro plugins for you. In Analog 3.x, the Vite plugins are separate but composable for Analog, Angular, and Nitro. Each plugin takes only the options it owns.

import { defineConfig } from 'vite';
import analog from '@analogjs/platform';
import angular from '@analogjs/vite-plugin-angular';
import nitro from '@analogjs/vite-plugin-nitro';

export default defineConfig(() => ({
  plugins: [
    analog({
      prerender: {
        routes: ['/', '/about'],
      },
    }),
    angular({
      inlineStylesExtension: 'scss',
    }),
    nitro({
      routeRules: { '/admin/**': { ssr: false } },
    }),
  ],
}));

This makes it clear where each option is configured, and lets you extend the plugins like any other Vite plugin. The ng update and nx migrate migrations split your existing config for you.

This also allows you to swap out the angular() plugin for the OXC Angular or Angular NGP plugin for compilation, while still using Analog features.

Support for Nitro v2 and Nitro v3 🔥

Analog uses Nitro for API routes and server deployment support. Nitro v2 remains the default through the @analogjs/vite-plugin-nitro package. Analog also adds support for the upcoming release of Nitro v3 as a standard Vite plugin.

To switch to Nitro v3, install the nitro package, and import nitro() from nitro/vite instead:

import analog from '@analogjs/platform';
import angular from '@analogjs/vite-plugin-angular';
import { nitro } from 'nitro/vite';

export default defineConfig(() => ({
  plugins: [analog(), angular(), nitro()],
}));

Analog detects and configures the correct Nitro version being used, so you can continue with the stable release of Nitro v2 and upgrade to Nitro v3 when you're ready.

Bring Your Own Server 🛒

In Analog 3.0, you can serve your Analog app from the server you already run (NestJS, Express, Fastify, Hono, or a plain Node http server) instead of Nitro. Your server owns the process and its routes. Analog handles server-side rendering, page endpoints and server functions inside it.

Point the new server option at your server's entry file:

// vite.config.ts
import analog from '@analogjs/platform';
import angular from '@analogjs/vite-plugin-angular';
import { defineConfig } from 'vite';

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [
    analog({ server: { entry: 'src/server/main.ts' } }),
    angular(),
  ],
});

Then mount Analog's handler with createAnalogHandler() from @analogjs/router/server, after your own routes:

// src/server/main.ts
import { createAnalogHandler } from '@analogjs/router/server';
import express from 'express';

const app = express();
app.get('/api/health', (req, res) => res.json({ ok: true }));
app.use(createAnalogHandler());

Fetch-native servers such as Hono use createAnalogRequestHandler(), which takes a Request and returns a Response, or null for requests Analog doesn't handle:

const handleAnalogRequest = createAnalogRequestHandler();

app.all('*', async (c) => (await handleAnalogRequest(c.req.raw)) ?? c.notFound());

Analog serves its own requests and passes everything else on with next(), so your 404 handling still applies. In development, Vite runs your server inside the dev server with HMR, and recreates the app when server code changes. In production, vite build outputs the client and a single server bundle you run with node dist/server/main.js.

NestJS Integration

There's a dedicated guide on using NestJS covering both the Express and Fastify adapters. Mount Analog in onModuleInit and your controllers keep priority. Server functions, page load functionality and SSR run inside the NestJS process too, so they can inject your NestJS services directly:

export const greet = serverFn(v.object({ name: v.string() }), async ({ name }) =>
  injectNest(GreetingService).greet(name),
);

Get started with the Custom Server guide and the NestJS integration guide.

Type-safe Routing 🧭

Analog introduces experimental type-safe routing, to further extend the Angular Router. Enable it with the experimental.typedRouting option:

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [
    analog({ experimental: { typedRouting: true } }),
    angular(),
    nitro()
  ],
});

Analog generates a route table from your pages, and checks paths and parameters in your templates and code.

Use the LinkTo directive in your templates for type-safety:

<a
  [linkTo]="{
    path: '/products/[id]',
    params: { id: product.id },
    query: { tab: 'details' }
  }"
>
  Details
</a>

For programmatic navigation or consumption of params, import the appropriate functions.

import { injectNavigate, injectParams } from '@analogjs/router';

const navigate = injectNavigate();
navigate('/products/[id]', { params: { id: 42 } });

const params = injectParams('/products/[id]');
// params().id is a string

With strictTemplates enabled, invalid routes and parameters used in the template now surface compilation errors to ensure correctness.

API routes also get validation with defineApiRoute, using any Standard Schema library such as Zod, Valibot, or ArkType:

// src/server/routes/api/users.post.ts
import { defineApiRoute } from '@analogjs/router/server/actions';
import { z } from 'zod';

export default defineApiRoute({
  body: z.object({ name: z.string().min(1) }),
  handler: ({ body }) => ({ name: body.name }),
});

Invalid requests return a 422 response with the validation issues, without calling the handler.

Supporting the Future of Angular Compilation with Vite ⚙️

Angular has recently introduced a new experimental hybrid preprocessor (NGP) using Rust and OXC, improving compilation performance of Angular applications, and integration with TypeScript 7 type-checking. This also improves support for plugins and integrations to support Angular compilation with different toolchains, including Vite.

Analog supports Angular's experimental hybrid preprocessor, with TypeScript 7 and Angular template type checking enabled by default.

To enable it, use the compilation option in the plugin:

angular({
  compilation: 'ngp'
});

Using a custom type-checker, such as the Rust-based TypeScript 7 type checker tsrs is also supported.

To enable, install the tsrs package, and set the typeChecker to tsrs:

angular({
  compilation: 'ngp',
  typeChecker: 'tsrs',
});

The Analog Vite Plugin for Angular will continue to receive updates as the new Angular compiler architecture matures.

Streaming SSR 🌊

Analog adds experimental streaming server-side rendering. Instead of waiting for the whole page to render, the server sends the document head right away, and sends each @defer (hydrate …) block as soon as it's ready.

Enable it in the Vite config:

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [
    analog({ experimental: { streaming: true } }),
    angular(),
    nitro(),
  ],
});

And update the render function to renderStream in the main.server.ts:

// src/main.server.ts
import { renderStream } from '@analogjs/router/server';
import { config } from './app/app.config.server';
import { AppComponent } from './app/app.component';

export default renderStream(AppComponent, config);

Then wrap content in @defer blocks with a hydrate trigger:

<h1>Dashboard</h1>

@defer (hydrate on viewport) {
  <app-recommendations />
} @placeholder {
  <p>Loading recommendations…</p>
}

SSR Streaming builds on Angular's incremental hydration. It falls back to buffered rendering for SEO/bot requests automatically. It requires Angular v21 or later.

Vite Plugin Integrations 🧩

Any Vite plugin can now hook into Angular compilation through a new analog.setup hook. Plugins can register component stylesheet preprocessors, control which files Angular compiles, and serve component styles through Vite's CSS pipeline.

For example, Tailwind CSS needs a @reference to your root stylesheet in each component stylesheet that uses @apply. A small Vite plugin can add it for you, and have @tailwindcss/vite process component styles during development:

import type { AnalogIntegrationPlugin } from '@analogjs/vite-plugin-angular';

export function angularTailwind(
  rootStylesheet: string,
): AnalogIntegrationPlugin {
  const inject = (code: string) =>
    code.includes('@apply') && !/^\s*@reference\b/m.test(code)
      ? `@reference "${rootStylesheet}";\n${code}`
      : code;

  return {
    name: 'angular-tailwind',
    enforce: 'pre',
    analog: {
      setup(ctx) {
        ctx.registerStylePreprocessor(inject);
        ctx.externalizeComponentStyles();
      },
    },
  };
}

You add the plugin to plugins: [...] like any other Vite plugin, with no extra Analog options:

import { resolve } from 'node:path';
import { defineConfig } from 'vite';
import analog from '@analogjs/platform';
import angular from '@analogjs/vite-plugin-angular';
import nitro from '@analogjs/vite-plugin-nitro';
import tailwindcss from '@tailwindcss/vite';

import { angularTailwind } from './tools/angular-tailwind';

export default defineConfig(() => ({
  plugins: [
    analog(),
    angular(),
    nitro(),
    tailwindcss(),
    angularTailwind(resolve(import.meta.dirname, 'src/styles.css')),
  ],
}));

See the Tailwind CSS guide and the Style Pipeline guide for more details.

AI Coding Agent Support 🤖

Analog ships guidance for AI coding agents with the framework, so the agent follows the conventions for the version you have installed.

  • @analogjs/platform includes an AGENTS.md file covering file-based routing, server and API routes, data fetching, content routes, and the modern Angular style Analog expects.
  • The same guidance ships as an analogjs skill in an Agent Plugins v1.0.0 manifest at node_modules/@analogjs/platform.
  • New projects from create-analog and the Nx generators include AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md files that point to the guidance in node_modules, so it stays up to date when you upgrade.

The Analog docs are readily available for agents to read:

  • llms.txt indexes the docs, and llms-full.txt contains all of them in one file.
  • Each docs section has its own llms.txt, such as https://analogjs.org/docs/features/llms.txt.
  • Add .md to any docs page URL to get that page as Markdown, or use the Copy page button to paste it into your AI assistant.

See the Build with AI guide for more details.

Also try Graft, a new OSS tool for managing patches, forks, and upstream changes automatically with agents.

Vite Ecosystem Upgrades ⚡️

Analog continues to integrate and support many Vite ecosystem integrations:

  • Angular v20-v22
  • Vite 6.x, 7.x, and 8.x, including Rolldown and OXC
  • Vitest 4.x and 5.x
  • Nx 21.2+ through Nx 24.x
  • Storybook 10.x
  • Astro 6.x, 7.x

Upgrading to Analog 3.0 🚀

Analog 3.0 requires Angular v20 or newer. Projects that need to stay on Angular v17-v19 can stay on Analog 2.x.

To upgrade, run the update command for your workspace:

ng update @analogjs/platform@latest

nx migrate @analogjs/platform@latest

The migrations handle the Vite config changes. For the full list of breaking changes, including removed APIs and new defaults, see the migration guide. The guide also includes a prompt you can give to an AI coding agent to run the migration for you.

Contributions and Community 🤓

AnalogJS would not be where it is without a team of core contributors and collaborators. Also thanks to the nearly 200 contributors to the project, whether through code, documentation, tests, or even just trying out the project.

The project has reached over 2 million monthly downloads on NPM, 3000 stars on GitHub, 1000+ members on Discord, 1000+ followers on Twitter/X.

Partner with Analog 🤝

Continued development of Analog would not be possible without our partners and community. Thanks to our official deployment partner Zerops, longtime supporters Snyder Technologies, Nx, new sponsor CodeRabbit, and many other backers of the project.

Find out more information on our partnership opportunities or reach out directly to partnerships[at]analogjs.org.

Join the Community 🥇

articles.title: Local Means Local: Test Firebase AI Logic Fallback Before Dispatch
articles.description: A button labeled “Run on this device” makes a concrete promise about where its input will be...
articles.body_html:
A button labeled “Run on this device” makes a concrete promise about where its input will be processed. A configuration named PREFER_ON_DEVICE makes a materially different promise: try the local model, then permit cloud inference when needed.

Both behaviors can be useful. The application needs to choose deliberately and describe the consequence before dispatching the request.

Firebase AI Logic exposes explicit inference modes for this choice. This walkthrough adds a small TypeScript policy in front of the SDK, verifies that disallowed requests never reach the provider adapter, and records the actual inference source when a live request succeeds. The key rule is simple: permission must constrain dispatch, not merely explain the response afterward.

Choose a mode that matches the interaction

The documented modes have different fallback behavior:

Mode Preference If that route is unavailable
ONLY_ON_DEVICE Local inference Error
PREFER_ON_DEVICE Local inference Cloud fallback
ONLY_IN_CLOUD Cloud inference Error
PREFER_IN_CLOUD Cloud inference Local fallback

An availability probe can improve the explanation, but it cannot substitute for a policy. Availability can change between the probe and execution. Use the mode itself to constrain the SDK’s permitted route.

Also keep the supported operation narrow. The current hybrid documentation distinguishes single-turn local generation from capabilities such as multi-turn chat and tool use. A feature supported by the cloud model does not automatically become a local capability.

Bind permission to the text being sent

The example offers local-only, local-preferred, and cloud-only choices. A cloud-capable choice requires an explicit grant for the current input. Changing that input invalidates the grant.

type Consent = { input: string; expiresAt: number };

function chooseMode(
  choice: "local-only" | "local-preferred" | "cloud-only",
  input: string,
  consent: Consent | undefined,
  now: number
) {
  if (choice === "local-only") return "ONLY_ON_DEVICE";
  if (!consent || consent.input !== input || consent.expiresAt <= now) {
    throw new Error("Cloud permission is missing or no longer valid.");
  }
  return choice === "cloud-only"
    ? "ONLY_IN_CLOUD"
    : "PREFER_ON_DEVICE";
}

This in-memory grant is an application UX rule. It is not server authorization, a legal consent record, or protection against compromised page JavaScript. A production product might bind the decision to additional context, such as the destination, attachments, and purpose.

The important implementation detail is ordering: validate the policy before constructing a provider request. Discovering the inference source after the response is too late to ask whether the input may leave the device.

Figure 1. Permission constrains dispatch. The returned inference source explains what happened afterward.

Keep the SDK adapter small

The companion pins Firebase 13.3.0 and typechecks this adapter against the installed declarations:

const ai = getAI(app, { backend: new GoogleAIBackend() });
const model = getGenerativeModel(ai, {
  mode: InferenceMode[mode],
  inCloudParams: { model: cloudModel },
});
const result = await model.generateContent(input);
return {
  text: result.response.text(),
  source: result.response.inferenceSource,
};

The imports come from firebase/ai; the complete module is supplied with the lab. Pass an explicitly selected cloud model rather than depending indefinitely on the SDK’s default. Keep an unreported source visibly unknown instead of inferring it from response speed.

There is deliberately no catch block that retries a failed local-only request using a cloud model. If the person chooses local-only and local inference fails, keep the source text and explain the failure. A subsequent cloud request is a separate user decision.

Verify the policy without provider credentials

The policy accepts an injected provider function. That lets the tests count dispatches without sending any text anywhere.

The executed tests establish that missing permission, expired permission, and permission for different text all block a cloud-capable request before the mock provider runs. A local-only provider failure propagates without a second call. A valid grant selects the intended SDK mode.

These results verify the application policy. They do not establish which route Firebase selects on a particular device or whether a generated answer is useful.

The visible policy panel is labeled as a fixture. Its “Mock provider calls” counter must not be presented as evidence of a live Firebase request. The real adapter remains available for the connected experiment.

Complete the live setup deliberately

Create or select a Firebase project, enable AI Logic, choose a provider, and configure App Check. Use its debug provider for local development and an appropriate production provider before deployment. Follow the current browser instructions for local inference, including model preparation and any required flags.

Keep Firebase configuration separate from server secrets. A Firebase web configuration is not a reason to place a Gemini provider secret in frontend code. Follow the selected Firebase provider’s credential setup rather than adapting a server-only Gemini example by exposing its key.

For the live matrix, record the requested mode, permission state, supported input type, actual source, success or error, and relevant request evidence. Run local-unavailable/cloud-allowed, local-unavailable/cloud-declined, local-ready, and disconnected cases. A cloud failure with no usable local model is a legitimate outcome.

Describe the boundary precisely

The phrase “on-device” can describe model inference without describing every request made by the application. Authentication, analytics, configuration, and model downloads have their own network behavior. Inspect them separately before making a whole-application privacy claim.

Likewise, a fixture test is valuable because it isolates the policy, but it cannot certify SDK fallback. This draft’s live Firebase matrix requires project credentials and browser execution; no provider routing or latency results are claimed.

A good fallback preserves a useful interaction while respecting the choice the person made. What should your application do when its preferred model is unavailable and the alternative changes where the input is processed?

References

  • Firebase hybrid configuration
  • Firebase hybrid web setup and limitations
  • Firebase App Check for AI Logic
  • Chrome Prompt API

articles.title: I tested Context7 on 6 libraries that changed in 2026
articles.description: Ten runs out of ten, my coding agent wrote a Vitest test that looked right and failed. The test I...
articles.body_html:
Ten runs out of ten, my coding agent wrote a Vitest test that looked right and failed. The test I wanted was twelve lines long. The bug was a default that Vitest 5 changed in September, and the model had no idea.

Sponsored by Upstash.

Context7 is an MCP server from Upstash that hands a coding agent up to date, version-specific library docs while it works.

To measure how often stale training data breaks agent code, I ran Claude Code headless (model alias sonnet) on six libraries whose APIs changed in 2026, once with plain file tools and once with Context7 added. The code, tasks, checks and all 120 raw runs live in thegdsks/docs-ab-bench.

TL;DR

Told to use Context7, the agent passed 44 of 45 runs on libraries that changed in 2026, against 35 of 45 for the plain agent on the same batches. The catch: with the tool installed and no instruction to use it, the agent barely called it and scored like the plain agent.

Vitest 5 changed the clearMocks default, and the agent missed it

The task reads like a junior ticket. Create a vi.fn() handler, call notify(handler) once in a beforeAll hook, then assert the handler ran exactly once. Years of Vitest tutorials teach this shape, so the model writes it from memory:

// src/notify.test.js
import { beforeAll, expect, test, vi } from 'vitest'
import { notify } from './notify.js'

const handler = vi.fn()

beforeAll(() => {
  notify(handler)
})

test('handler is called exactly once', () => {
  expect(handler).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1)
})

On Vitest 4.1.12 that passes. On 5.0.3 it fails. Version 5.0.0 made clearMocks: true the default, so Vitest now clears call history before every test and the assertion never sees the call from beforeAll:

FAIL  src/notify.test.js > handler is called exactly once
AssertionError: expected "vi.fn()" to be called 1 times, but got 0 times

The fix is one line of config, if you know the default moved:

// vitest.config.js
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config'

// Vitest 5 clears mock history before every test; keep the beforeAll call visible.
export default defineConfig({
  test: { clearMocks: false },
})

Against the repo's fixture (src/notify.js), the test fails without this config and passes with it.

The plain agent failed this 10 of 10 times in one pass mode. Given Context7 and this one extra line in the prompt, it passed 5 of 5:

"Before you write code, use the Context7 tools to look up the current documentation for the libraries involved."

The harness changes one thing: the MCP config

Both arms get the same task text, system prompt, model and file tools. The baseline arm starts Claude Code with an empty server list and --strict-mcp-config, so it cannot pick up any docs server from my machine. The Context7 arm gets the remote Context7 server and nothing else.

Every run starts in a fresh temp folder with the library version pinned. When the agent stops, the subject's own check.sh runs inside that folder and exits 0 or 1. For Vitest it greps the test file for a mock assertion and a beforeAll, then reads the JSON report from vitest run. Nobody judges the code by vibes, me included.

I ran two modes. One pass mode (oneshot) gives the agent file tools only and no way to run anything. Agentic mode adds a shell for npm, npx and node, so the agent can run the tests and read the error.

Each subject also ships a correct and a stale reference solution. A verify command confirms the untouched fixture fails, the correct answer passes and the stale one fails. If a check could not fail, a pass would mean nothing.

Every result, with and without Context7

Library Mode Baseline Context7, told to use it Context7, not told
Vitest 5 oneshot 0 of 5 5 of 5 2 of 5
Vitest 5 agentic 3 of 5 5 of 5 not run
SvelteKit 3 oneshot 4 of 5 5 of 5 3 of 5
SvelteKit 3 agentic 5 of 5 5 of 5 not run
AI SDK 7 oneshot 5 of 5 5 of 5 5 of 5
AI SDK 7 agentic 5 of 5 5 of 5 not run
React Router 8 oneshot 3 of 5 5 of 5 not run
Astro 7 oneshot 5 of 5 4 of 5 not run
TypeScript 6 oneshot 5 of 5 5 of 5 not run

I ran the one pass baseline twice with an identical prompt, so pooled it comes to 0 of 10 for Vitest 5, 8 of 10 for SvelteKit 3 and 10 of 10 for AI SDK 7. React Router 8 swapped data for loaderData in meta args, and Astro 7 now needs @astrojs/markdown-remark for remark plugins. The Wilson intervals for the hinted cells run from 88 to 100 percent for Context7 and 64 to 87 percent for the baseline. They do not overlap, barely.

With a shell, SvelteKit 3 needs no docs tool

SvelteKit 3 stopped reading svelte.config.js and moved config into the sveltekit() Vite plugin. It also removed $app/stores in favor of $app/state. In one pass mode the plain agent got 8 of 10.

Give it a shell and both arms pass 5 of 5. The plain agent can run the build and read the error. A loud break documents itself.

Vitest shows the opposite case. A cleared mock produces no import error and no deprecation warning, only an assertion that says zero calls. With a shell the plain agent climbed to 3 of 5, and the Context7 arm held at 5 of 5. Silent behavior changes are where looking up the docs first pays off.

When the model already knows the library, docs cost tokens

AI SDK 7 and TypeScript 6 changed too, yet the model handled both alone. Both arms passed 5 of 5 everywhere. On Astro 7 the result flipped by one run, 4 of 5 for Context7 against 5 of 5 for the baseline. I count that as noise, and it stays in the table.

Context7 does little until you tell the agent to use it

My first Context7 batch had no hint. The agent had the tool and barely touched it, at 0.6 calls per run on Vitest 5 and SvelteKit 3 and zero on AI SDK 7. The results looked like the baseline: 2 of 5 on Vitest, 3 of 5 on SvelteKit.

With the one line hint the agent made about 2 calls per run, one to each of the server's two tools (resolve-library-id and query-docs), and Vitest went to 5 of 5. The official npx ctx7 setup also installs a skill meant to trigger Context7 on library questions. My harness used the bare server without it, so the no-hint column covers a bare install only.

What up to date docs cost in tokens

Mean tokens per run, rounded down to the thousand. Claude Code counts cache reads and writes as input, so these are totals, not fresh tokens.

Library and mode Baseline Context7, told to use it
Vitest 5, one pass 35k 64k
Vitest 5, with a shell 105k 98k
SvelteKit 3, one pass 83k 67k
SvelteKit 3, with a shell 49k 74k
AI SDK 7, with a shell 95k 105k
TypeScript 6, one pass 37k 52k
Astro 7, one pass 160k 148k

The cheapest Vitest run is the baseline at 35k tokens, and it fails every time. Docs cost extra where the model already knew the API. Upstash's own benchmark against web search reports about 37 percent fewer tokens and about 35 percent lower cost per query. Upstash wrote it and it skips answer quality, so I keep it apart from mine.

My first harness was unfair to the plain agent

The first shell mode allowed a short list of commands, and a refused command ended the run. The plain agent wrote a stale config file, saw the build error, then tried to delete the file. Delete was not on the list, so the run stopped. The Context7 arm never wrote the stale file.

The giveaway: the plain agent scored worse with a shell than without one. I threw that batch away and rebuilt the shell inside a sandbox, where writes stay in the project folder and network only reaches the package registry. No number here comes from the discarded batch.

Set up Context7 MCP in one command 

npx ctx7 setup

It runs OAuth, creates an API key and installs a skill for your agent. It needs Node 22.13 or newer. The free plan gives you 1,000 calls per month, and Pro costs $10 per seat per month with 2,000 calls per seat. At about 2 calls per task, that stretches far.

If you run the MCP server locally instead, pin it. CVE-2026-75130, a prompt injection through the Custom AI Instructions feature, got its fix in context7-mcp 2.1.3, so anything older should go. For Claude Code, save this as .mcp.json in your project root. Create a free key in the Context7 dashboard and export it as CONTEXT7_API_KEY:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "context7": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "@upstash/context7-mcp@4.7.3"],
      "env": { "CONTEXT7_API_KEY": "${CONTEXT7_API_KEY}" }
    }
  }
}

The API guide covers keys and rate limits. Then add the hint to your agent's instructions file, such as CLAUDE.md, unless the setup skill covers it.

Reproduce the benchmark on your machine

You need the Node version listed in the repo README and the Claude Code CLI, installed and logged in.

git clone https://github.com/thegdsks/docs-ab-bench
cd docs-ab-bench
npm install
cp .env.example .env
npx tsx src/cli.ts verify --subject vitest-5
npx tsx src/cli.ts report --batch headline-oneshot-hint
BENCH_DOCS_HINT=1 npx tsx src/cli.ts run --subject vitest-5 --arm both --n 5 --mode oneshot --driver claude-code --model sonnet --batch mine
npx tsx src/cli.ts report --batch mine

The first verify installs the pinned dependencies once and caches them. The first report reads my shipped runs for free (ls runs lists every batch), while run spends your own Claude Code usage. Put CONTEXT7_API_KEY in .env if you have one. Drop BENCH_DOCS_HINT=1 and pick a new batch name to see the unprompted behavior, or add --mode agentic for the sandboxed shell.

Where these numbers stop

Five runs per cell is small. One 5 of 5 cell leaves a wide interval, so I lean on the pooled 44 of 45 and the 0 of 10. I used one model through one agent driver. I also wrote the tasks myself, and I picked libraries known to have changed, so the setup favors a docs tool by design. On a library your model already knows, my own data says you will usually pay extra tokens for nothing.

What Context7 changes in the code your agent writes

Context7 serves the agent current docs for a library, for a specific version if you name it, at the moment it needs them. In my runs that came down to four effects.

Current syntax instead of remembered syntax

The Vitest 5 failures were a stale default, not a made-up function. With the docs in context the agent wrote against the new clearMocks default and passed 5 of 5.

Fewer bugs from changes after the model's training

SvelteKit 3 moved config out of svelte.config.js. In one pass the plain agent got 8 of 10 and the Context7 agent got 5 of 5.

Docs that match your version

A Context7 library id can carry a version, in the form /owner/repo/<version>, so you can point the agent at the release in your lockfile and not only the latest one.

A lookup to check against

A model's wrong answer and its right answer sound the same. Reading the docs gives it something to verify instead of recall.

Upstash describes the aim as fewer outdated or hallucinated APIs. I measured the outdated kind and did not test for invented ones.

Context7 FAQ

Does Context7 reduce hallucinations in generated code?

It cut the outdated-API failures in my runs, for example 0 of 10 to 5 of 5 on Vitest 5. I did not test for invented functions, so I cannot say it removes those.

Does Context7 work if you do not tell the agent to use it?

Barely, as a bare MCP server. Without the hint the agent averaged 0.6 calls per run on Vitest 5 and scored 2 of 5. I did not test the setup skill.

Does Context7 cost more tokens?

Sometimes. On TypeScript 6 the mean rose from 37k to 52k tokens with no change in passes, while on Vitest 5 with a shell it fell from 105k to 98k.

Is Context7 safe to install?

Pin a local server to context7-mcp 2.1.3 or later, which fixes CVE-2026-75130. The hosted server needs no pin.

Bottom line

Install Context7, then make sure something tells the agent to use it. That one line took my agent from 0 of 10 to 5 of 5 on a Vitest default that throws no error. If a library you depend on is missing, you can add it to Context7. What silent default in your stack would your agent still get wrong today?

Originally published at thegdsks.com.

Context7 and Upstash names and logos are trademarks of Upstash, Inc., shown because this is a sponsored post about their product.

articles.title: I Captured 89 Product Pages in Less Than 30 Seconds. Then Codex Built the Presentation.
articles.description: How I used Playwright to capture product pages and gave Codex the screenshots and GitHub backlog to build an editable PowerPoint deck.
articles.body_html:
In the first article in this series, I described how I take a product from a brainstorm to a production release with AI. In the follow-up about finding the first users, I wrote about the difficulty of reaching beyond my LinkedIn circles.

Explaining the product is part of that work. Someone encountering it for the first time needs to see what they could do with it. This article looks at how I collected the product visuals and reused them in a presentation.

I needed current screenshots of a product I am building. Not three polished pages for a landing page, but every routable page in the application, including the ones that were not linked from the navigation.

Doing that manually would have been a small project of its own: find the routes, open each page, wait for it to render, take a full-page screenshot, name the file, and keep track of what I had missed.

Instead, I gave the job to GPT-6 Luna with Playwright.

The result from my run was 89 screenshots in less than 30 seconds, using 1.76 credits.

That is close enough to free for a task that would normally consume hours of repetitive attention. More importantly, those screenshots did not remain a folder of images. I later gave them to Codex together with the GitHub issues and epics for the product, then used its PowerPoint integration to create an editable presentation.

The useful lesson was not simply that a small model was cheap. It was that the inexpensive step created evidence for the more demanding step that followed.

The screenshot task was repetitive, but not trivial

"Take screenshots of my application" would have been an easy prompt to write and a bad one to trust.

An agent could visit the home page and the pages exposed in the main menu, save a few files, and report success. That might look convincing while missing secondary routes, pages still under development, or screens reachable only through a direct URL.

I needed a result I could inspect, count, and reuse. This was the prompt:

Use Playwright to visit every routable page in the app, including pages not linked in the navigation. Take a full-page screenshot of each page and save the PNGs under docs/screenshots/. Name each file with a two-digit number followed by a descriptive route name, ordered by the app's navigation menu; place pages that aren't in the menu afterward. Use a consistent desktop viewport, wait for each page to finish rendering before capturing it, and verify that every route was visited and every screenshot was saved. Don't include reusable components or partials as separate pages.

The wording matters because each clause closes a predictable gap.

"Every routable page" forces the agent to inspect the application rather than behave like a visitor clicking through the menu. Calling out pages that are not in the navigation makes that expectation explicit. Full-page capture prevents a collection of arbitrary viewport crops, while the naming convention makes 89 files reviewable without manually sorting them afterward.

The last sentence establishes the boundary. I wanted user-facing pages, not every component or partial that happened to exist in the codebase.

It is a prompt, but it behaves more like a small specification. The output location, order, file format, viewport behavior, completion condition, and exclusions are all visible. That makes the task suitable for a low-cost model because success does not depend on whether I like the prose of its final answer. I can check the files.

Why I used GPT-6 Luna

I do not need the most capable model for every task.

This job required tool use, persistence, and basic interpretation of the application's route structure. It did not require a product strategy, a nuanced argument, or a presentation narrative. Once the route boundary was clear, the rest was a mechanical browser operation.

That made GPT-6 Luna a reasonable choice. In this particular run, it completed the capture with 1.76 credits. I am deliberately describing that as a measured result, not a permanent price promise: credit systems and model behavior can change.

The economic point still holds. Model selection should follow the work. If a cheaper model can complete a bounded task and the result can be verified independently, paying for more reasoning does not automatically produce more value.

The important word is verified.

For a screenshot job, I want to check at least four things:

  • The route list matches the application.
  • The expected number of PNG files exists.
  • The images use the intended viewport and have plausible dimensions.
  • None of the pages was captured in a loading, error, empty, or signed-out state.

A folder containing 89 files proves that 89 files were created. It does not prove that every page is correct. Authentication, role-specific routes, feature flags, dynamic parameters, and slow data loading can all make a screenshot set look complete when it is not.

The screenshots became a product artifact

The surprise was not the speed. It was how useful the folder became afterward.

Product screenshots are often treated as disposable material for documentation or marketing. This set was closer to a visual inventory. It showed the product as it existed across 89 routes at one moment, including screens I would not have selected for a polished demo.

That distinction matters when a product is still under development. The navigation shows what users can reach easily. The route inventory shows what the application contains. The GitHub roadmap shows what I intend to build. Those are three different views, and they do not always agree.

The screenshots gave me the current implementation. My GitHub issues and epics contained the intent behind it: planned capabilities, larger product themes, and work that might not yet be visible in the interface.

Together, they formed better input for a presentation than a prompt such as "create a deck about my product."

Why I switched to Codex for the presentation

The next task was no longer mechanical.

A useful product presentation needs selection. It has to decide which screens explain the product, how they support the story, where the current implementation ends, and where the roadmap begins. It also needs visual hierarchy, consistent layouts, and an editable output that I can continue working with.

The audience changes that selection. For the walkthrough I discussed in the previous article, I would choose the screens that explain one task a prospective user cares about. A stakeholder presentation may also need the roadmap and the reasoning behind planned work. The same screenshot inventory can support both, with a different story and a different scope.

This is where I preferred Codex. Its integration with PowerPoint is particularly useful because the result is a real presentation rather than a textual outline pretending to be one. Codex could work from the screenshots, inspect the GitHub issues and epics, structure the product story, and place the visual evidence into an editable deck.

The two sources played different roles:

  • The screenshots showed what existed.
  • GitHub showed the tracked product direction.

That reduced a common failure in generated decks: confidently describing a product that exists only in the prompt. The presentation could be grounded in the interface while still explaining what I was developing next.

It still required review. Issues can be outdated, a screenshot can show an unfinished state, and a model can create a clean narrative by hiding contradictions that the product team actually needs to discuss. I checked the deck against both sources rather than treating the generated slides as the source of truth.

Cheap execution and expensive judgment

I see these as two different classes of work.

The screenshot task was bounded and countable. There was a route list, a folder, a naming rule, and a file count. GPT-6 Luna did not need to understand why page 47 mattered to the product strategy. It needed to open the page correctly and save the image in the right place.

The presentation task required judgment. Which screenshots belong together? Which GitHub issues explain a visible workflow? What should a viewer understand after ten minutes? Which roadmap items are plans rather than shipped features? Those questions benefit from stronger reasoning and a tool that can implement the answer directly in PowerPoint.

Using one model for both jobs would have been simpler to describe, but not necessarily better. The handoff between them was the useful design:

  1. Use Playwright to turn the running product into a verified screenshot set.
  2. Preserve that set under docs/screenshots/ as a reusable project artifact.
  3. Combine the visual inventory with GitHub issues and epics.
  4. Use Codex and the PowerPoint integration for synthesis and implementation.
  5. Review the deck against the application and the issue tracker.

The low-cost step did not compete with the higher-value step. It improved its input.

What I would tighten before running it again

The original prompt worked well, but there are a few controls I would add for a production workflow.

First, I would ask for a route manifest next to the PNG files, recording the route, filename, page title, HTTP status, and capture result. That would make the coverage easier to audit than relying on filenames alone.

Second, I would define how authenticated and parameterized routes should be handled. A route such as /projects/:id is not one page in practice, and different roles may see different interfaces at the same URL.

Third, I would add an explicit privacy check. Screenshots can capture test customers, email addresses, tokens, internal URLs, or other information that should never enter a public article or presentation.

Finally, I would separate capture from approval. The agent can create the inventory, but a human should decide which screens are safe, current, and useful enough to leave the repository.

The practical takeaway

The 1.76-credit result is a good hook, but it is not the main reason I will reuse this workflow.

The real value came from choosing tools according to the shape of the work. GPT-6 Luna handled a repetitive browser task with a clear definition of done. Codex handled the part that required product context, narrative choices, GitHub evidence, and a polished PowerPoint artifact.

If you are building a product, do not start the presentation with a blank slide and a vague prompt. Start by capturing what the product actually is. Then connect that evidence to the work you have planned.

The cheapest useful model can create the evidence that makes the more capable model worth using.
