Floppy Disk Vibes in 2026

C# 15 is here, and one of its new features has such an old-school vibe, it could come with a floppy disk.

Yes, I'm talking about labeled break and continue, also known as labeled loops.

Wait, what's a floppy disk?

If you don't know what a floppy disk is, congratulations, you're probably still in your 20s. Here's what they look like:

And yes, those are mine. They still work.

Though I'm not that old. I just stepped into my 30s, which makes me a proud millennial. Old enough to remember floppy disks, young enough that my knees only complain after leg day.

Holding working floppy disks in 2026 feels exactly like using labeled loops in C# 15. Both are technology from another era, both still do their job perfectly, and both make you wonder: "Wait, why does this feel new?"

24 Years Late to the Party

This feature is about 24 years late to the party. C# 1.0 shipped in 2002, and this feels like something that should have been in the box on day one.

Here's why it feels so late. C# was heavily inspired by Java (with a good dose of C++), and Java has had labeled loops since its very first release in 1996. Thirty years ago. In Java, breaking out of a nested loop has always looked like this:

outer:
for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
    for (int j = 0; j < 5; j++) {
        if (i * j == 6) {
            System.out.println("Found it: " + i + " x " + j);
            break outer; // exits BOTH loops
        }
    }
}

One label, one break outer;, and you're out of both loops. No flags, no tricks, no drama. Easy.

The Nested Loop Tax

Meanwhile, C# developers spent more than two decades writing this:

bool found = false;

for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++)
{
    for (int j = 0; j < 5; j++)
    {
        if (i * j == 6)
        {
            Console.WriteLine($"Found it: {i} x {j}");
            found = true;
            break; // only exits the inner loop...
        }
    }

    if (found)
        break; // ...so we need a second break for the outer one
}

If you've written C# for more than a week, you've written this. We all have. It's the nested loop tax.

Wait, C# Already Had Labels?

Here's something even weirder: C# has had labels since day one. They just had exactly one job: being a target for goto.

For anyone who hasn't seen goto in the wild (lucky you), here's how it works in C#:

for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++)
{
    for (int j = 0; j < 5; j++)
    {
        if (i * j == 6)
        {
            Console.WriteLine($"Found it: {i} x {j}");
            goto done; // jump straight to the label below
        }
    }
}

done:
Console.WriteLine("Out of the loops!");

You put a label in the method (done:), and goto done; teleports execution there. It works, and it solves the nested loop problem, but goto has a reputation... a bad one. A really, really bad one. Don't use it. Just don't.

The problem with goto is that it can jump almost anywhere in the method. The label can be above you, below you, or 200 lines away, so you have to go hunting for it to understand what happens next. Your code can get messy really fast.

Enter C# 15

C# 15 takes those same labels and lets break and continue use them:

outer:
for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++)
{
    for (int j = 0; j < 5; j++)
    {
        if (i * j == 6)
        {
            Console.WriteLine($"Found it: {i} x {j}");
            break outer; // exits BOTH loops
        }
    }
}

Look familiar? It's almost character-for-character the Java version from earlier.

Labeled break vs goto

The key difference from goto is that the label sits on the loop itself, and break outer; can only target a loop (or switch) that you're currently inside. You can't jump to random places or into the middle of something else. It's controlled, structured, and the intent is obvious just from reading the line: "get me out of the outer loop."

bool flag goto Labeled break
Extra state to track Yes No No
Can jump anywhere No Almost 😬 No, only to enclosing loops or switch
Intent readable at the jump Meh Not really Yes
Gets you side-eye in code review Sometimes Always We'll see...

So... How Do I Feel About It?

To be honest, I don't know yet.

Part of me thinks it's weird. Labels have always meant "goto lives here, be careful," and that reflex is hard to unlearn.

But another part of me kinda likes it. It makes the code simpler. The flag variable is gone, the second break is gone, and the logic reads exactly the way I'd explain it out loud.

The truth is, I haven't used it enough in real-world code to make up my mind (duh... it's a brand-new feature). So in this article, I'm going to do what I do with every new feature: poke it, push it, and see where it shines and where it starts to smell.

Let's unpack it.

Meet Labeled continue

So far, we've only talked about break. But continue got the same upgrade, and it might be the more useful of the two.

A regular continue skips to the next iteration of the innermost loop. A labeled continue skips to the next iteration of whichever loop you name.

Let's say we're packing orders, and if any item in an order is out of stock, we want to skip the entire order and move on to the next one:

string[][] orders =
[
    ["Keyboard", "Mouse"],
    ["Monitor", "OUT_OF_STOCK", "Cable"],
    ["Headphones"]
];

nextOrder:
foreach (string[] order in orders)
{
    Console.WriteLine("New order:");

    foreach (string item in order)
    {
        if (item == "OUT_OF_STOCK")
        {
            Console.WriteLine("  Item missing, skipping this order.");
            continue nextOrder; // jump to the next ORDER, not the next item
        }

        Console.WriteLine($"  Packing {item}");
    }

    Console.WriteLine("  Order shipped!");
}

Output:

Notice that the second order never prints "Order shipped!". The continue nextOrder; skipped the rest of the outer loop body and went straight to the next order.

Also notice the label name. I could've called it outer, but nextOrder makes continue nextOrder; read like plain English. Name your labels by intent, not by position. Future you will thank you.

How We Did It Before C# 15

Here's the same logic without labeled loops, the way we've been writing it for years:

foreach (string[] order in orders)
{
    Console.WriteLine("New order:");
    bool skipOrder = false;

    foreach (string item in order)
    {
        if (item == "OUT_OF_STOCK")
        {
            Console.WriteLine("  Item missing, skipping this order.");
            skipOrder = true;
            break; // step 1: get out of the inner loop...
        }

        Console.WriteLine($"  Packing {item}");
    }

    if (skipOrder)
        continue; // step 2: ...then skip the rest of the outer loop

    Console.WriteLine("  Order shipped!");
}

It works, but look at what it costs:

  • An extra variable whose only job is to carry a message from the inner loop to the outer one.
  • Two jumps instead of one: a break inside, then a continue outside.
  • A hidden trap: skipOrder has to be declared inside the outer loop so it resets for every order. Move it above the outer foreach, and after the first skipped order, every order after it gets skipped too. It still compiles, there's no warning, and the output is quietly wrong.

With C# 15, all of that collapses into a single line: continue nextOrder;. That's really what a labeled continue is: a break from the inner loop and a continue on the outer loop, in one statement.

Escaping a Loop From Inside a switch

This one has annoyed C# developers forever. Inside a switch, break belongs to the switch, not the loop around it. So if you want to exit the loop from within a case, a plain break won't help.

Labeled break fixes that:

string[] commands = ["move", "jump", "quit", "move"];

gameLoop:
foreach (string command in commands)
{
    switch (command)
    {
        case "move":
            Console.WriteLine("Moving...");
            break; // exits the switch only

        case "jump":
            Console.WriteLine("Jumping...");
            break; // exits the switch only

        case "quit":
            Console.WriteLine("Quitting the game.");
            break gameLoop; // exits the whole loop
    }
}

Output:

The last "move" never runs, because break gameLoop; jumped out of both the switch and the foreach.

The Rules of the Game

Labeled jumps are simple, but there are a few rules worth knowing before you start sprinkling labels everywhere.

Rule #1: break can target loops and switch. continue can only target loops.

That makes sense when you think about it. You can exit a switch, but there's no "next iteration" of a switch to continue to. So this won't compile:

mySwitch:
switch (value)
{
    case 1:
        continue mySwitch; // ❌ compile error: continue needs a loop
}

Rule #2: You can only jump to something you're inside.

Labeled break and continue only work with an enclosing loop or switch. You can't use them to jump sideways into another loop or to some random spot in the method. This is exactly what makes them safer than goto.

Rule #3: Watch out for stacked labels.

This is the sneaky one. C# technically lets you put more than one label in front of a statement:

first:
second:
for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++)
{
    for (int j = 0; j < 5; j++)
    {
        if (i * j == 6)
            break first; // ❌ compile error
    }
}

You might expect both labels to point to the for loop, but they don't. Only the label directly in front of the loop (second) labels the loop. first labels the second: for (...) labeled statement, which isn't a loop. So break first; fails to compile, while break second; works just fine.

Is this something you'll run into every day?
No.

Will it confuse someone on your team at 6 PM on a Friday?
Absolutely.

Rule #4: Without a label, nothing changes.

Plain break and continue work exactly as they always did. This feature is purely additive, so none of your existing code changes behavior.

Your IDE Already Wants You to Use It

Here's a fun surprise. .NET 11 comes with a new code style rule, IDE0410 ("Use labeled jump statement"), that looks for the old patterns: bool flags propagating a break outward, goto jumping past nested loops, and goto to an empty label at the end of a loop body. It then suggests replacing them with a labeled break or continue.

It's on by default for C# 15 projects. So if you open an old codebase full of found = true; break; patterns after upgrading, don't be surprised when your IDE lights up like a Christmas tree.

If you're not ready for that, you can turn it off in your .editorconfig:

[*.cs]
dotnet_diagnostic.IDE0410.severity = none

Wrapping Up

Labeled break and continue aren't flashy. They won't make headlines like union types did. But they fix a small, annoying problem that C# developers have been working around for 24 years.

Quick cheat sheet:

  • Use a labeled break to exit an outer loop, or a loop from inside a switch.
  • Use a labeled continue to skip to the next iteration of an outer loop.
  • Name labels by intent (nextOrder, gameLoop), not position (outer, loop1).
  • Avoid stacked labels.
  • Keep it simple: one label per loop nest is usually plenty.

So, do I like it? I think I do. It's like my floppy disks: retro, a little weird in 2026, but it still does its job perfectly.

All the code from this article is in my .NET 11 playground: dotnet11-playground. Feel free to clone it, break it, and contribute.

What about you? Are you going to use labeled loops, or do they give you goto flashbacks? Let me know in the comments. 👇

articles.body_html:
TL;DR

  • An agent gateway gives applications and agents one place to connect to model providers and tools. Depending on the project, it can also handle routing, retries, budgets, access controls, caching and request logs.
  • The nine gateways here take different approaches: Bifrost, Kong, Agent Router, Apache APISIX, LiteLLM, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, Azure API Management AI gateway, Cloudflare AI Gateway and Vercel AI Gateway.
  • Bifrost is a strong option for teams that want a self-hosted gateway with model, MCP and agent traffic controls. Its commercial Edge product can also route AI traffic from employee devices.
  • Agent support varies. Check each gateway's tool and protocol support, deployment model and feature boundaries before adopting it.

A few years ago, many teams adopted gateways to centralize provider keys and billing. Those needs have not gone away, but teams now also have to think about model choice, reliability, usage limits and the growing number of tools connected to agents.

The projects in this list are not interchangeable. Some focus on model routing, while others build AI features on top of a broader API or service-mesh stack. This article compares nine agent gateways, looking at how they handle models, tools, deployment and operational controls.

What an agent gateway does

At a basic level, an agent gateway is a shared point for traffic between applications, agents, model providers and tools. It can handle provider-specific formats, routing and retries across services such as OpenAI, Anthropic, AWS Bedrock and Google Vertex AI. Some gateways also manage MCP servers, tool permissions or agent-to-agent traffic.

Some projects add budgets, access controls, audit trails and caching. Others focus on getting requests to the right model with low operational overhead. The right choice depends on which of those jobs you need the gateway to do.

How to choose an agent gateway

  • Provider coverage. Confirm the providers and API formats your application needs today, then check how new providers are added.
  • Reliability and latency. Look for retries, fallbacks and load balancing. Treat benchmark numbers as a starting point.
  • Deployment and license. Check whether the gateway is self-hosted, managed or both, and distinguish open-source components from paid hosting, support or enterprise features.
  • Operations. Consider how the project handles secrets, budgets, access controls, logs and upgrades. A gateway still needs someone to run it.
  • MCP and agent support. If your applications call tools, check whether the gateway routes or governs MCP traffic, and how identity and permissions work.

The nine gateways at a glance

Here is the short version. Bifrost, LiteLLM, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, Azure API Management AI gateway, Cloudflare AI Gateway and Vercel AI Gateway focus on model traffic and related controls. Bifrost, Agent Router, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway and Azure API Management also offer options for agent and tool traffic. These nine gateways differ in agent support, deployment and feature boundaries.

Gateway Form factor Model coverage Routing and reliability Agent tooling Deployment A good fit when
Bifrost Standalone Go gateway 25+ providers, 10,000+ models Retries, fallbacks, load balancing Native MCP gateway and A2A Agent Gateway Self-hosted; Enterprise adds options You want one gateway for models and agents
Kong AI Gateway AI features in Kong Gateway Major hosted and self-hosted APIs Routing, load balancing, plugins AI MCP Proxy plugins Self-hosted or Konnect Kong already runs your APIs
Agent Router Envoy Gateway control plane and CLI Hosted and self-hosted providers Central routing, quotas and failover AI and MCP traffic Kubernetes or standalone CLI Your platform is built on Envoy
Apache APISIX API gateway with AI plugins OpenAI, Anthropic, Bedrock and more Multi-provider proxy, balancing and retries OpenAPI-to-MCP plugin Self-hosted You want an open-source API and AI gateway
LiteLLM Python SDK and proxy 100+ providers Routing, retries, fallbacks MCP gateway Self-hosted proxy Your stack is Python-first
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway Managed AI gateway Multiple model providers, APIs and tools Model-based routing and unified access MCP tools and A2A traffic AWS managed service You want a managed entry point for agents, tools and models
Azure API Management AI gateway AI features in API Management OpenAI, Anthropic, Vertex AI, Bedrock and more Load balancing, quotas and policies MCP servers and A2A agent APIs Azure API Management You want AI governance within Azure API Management
Cloudflare AI Gateway Managed gateway Multiple model providers Routing, retries and fallbacks Model gateway for agent applications Cloudflare You want managed routing and observability
Vercel AI Gateway Managed gateway Multiple model providers Routing and provider fallbacks Tool calls via supported models Hosted, usable from any cloud You want managed model access for apps and coding agents

The sections below look at what each project does well, where it fits and what to check before adopting it.

1. Bifrost: A gateway for models, MCP and agents

Bifrost is an open-source LLM gateway for enterprise AI, licensed under Apache 2.0 and written in Go. It provides one OpenAI-compatible interface to more than 10,000 models across 25+ providers. With its drop-in setup, an existing app can usually switch over by changing its base URL. Bifrost ships as a single binary and can run on a VM, in Kubernetes, in a private cloud or on a disconnected network.

Core capabilities

Performance is one of Bifrost's main selling points. Bifrost adds about 11 microseconds of overhead at 5,000 requests per second on a single t3.xlarge, with a 100% success rate. In an AWS EC2 comparison with 500 concurrent users over 60 seconds, Bifrost handled 424 requests per second while LiteLLM handled 44.84, with P99 latencies of 1.68 seconds and 90.72 seconds, respectively.

For governance, virtual keys let teams set budgets and rate limits by key, team, customer or model. The Enterprise tier connects to identity providers such as Okta, Microsoft Entra, Keycloak, Zitadel, Auth0 and Google Workspace, as well as other OIDC providers. It also adds SCIM 2.0 directory sync, detailed role-based access control, data access controls and reusable access profiles.

Routing supports weighted load balancing, retries with backoff and automatic fallbacks. Semantic caching, backed by Redis, Qdrant, Weaviate or Pinecone, can return stored answers for similar prompts.

The MCP gateway controls which MCP servers and tools agents can use. Access can be filtered at the client, request and virtual-key levels, with per-user OAuth so each person connects using their own account. Code Mode takes a different approach to large tool sets: instead of loading every tool definition into the model context, the model writes a short script to coordinate the tools it needs.

Code Mode reduces input token use by up to 92.8%. In a 508-tool test, Code Mode reduced costs from $377 to $29, with all tasks passing. The linked MCP gateway write-up has the full results.

Bifrost Edge extends those controls to AI tools running on employee devices. Available for macOS, Windows and Linux, it routes traffic from desktop chat apps, browser-based AI, terminal coding agents and their MCP servers through the Bifrost gateway after a one-time SSO sign-in. Edge routes AI traffic only and does not inspect other device activity.

Gateway virtual keys, budgets and guardrails can then apply to those tools, including content safety, PII and secret detection on requests and responses, as well as integrations with AWS Bedrock Guardrails, Azure Content Safety, Google Model Armor, CrowdStrike AIDR and Check Point Guard. Administrators can allow or block apps and MCP servers centrally. Rules are enforced on the device. Rollout can use existing device management tools such as Jamf, Intune, Kandji, Omnissa Workspace ONE or JumpCloud.

For regulated environments, the Enterprise tier adds clustering, adaptive load balancing with circuit breakers, signed audit logs, and integrations with AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager and HashiCorp Vault. It also supports in-VPC, on-premises and air-gapped deployments, where prompts and responses can stay within your infrastructure. Bifrost is SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001, HIPAA and GDPR compliant, and Fortune 500 companies run it in production across several industries.

Where it fits

Bifrost fits best when a team wants model, MCP and agent traffic controls in one gateway, especially in a self-hosted, VPC-isolated, on-premises or air-gapped environment.

Identity-based governance, clustering, adaptive load balancing, guardrail and vault integrations, and in-VPC deployment are part of the paid Enterprise tier, not the open-source core. Edge also requires an Enterprise gateway and is priced per endpoint.

A limited pilot can help validate the endpoint rollout before expanding it.

Best for: Teams that need to manage model, MCP and agent traffic from one gateway, especially when they have strict deployment or governance requirements. Bifrost supports self-hosted, VPC-isolated, on-premises and air-gapped environments.

💎 Check out the Bifrost repository ☆

2. Kong AI Gateway: AI features in an established API platform

Kong AI Gateway adds AI-specific features to Kong's established API gateway. If your APIs already run on Kong, you can use the same control plane, plugin model and operational setup for model traffic. The AI features include provider routing, token-based rate limits, prompt guard plugins, semantic caching and semantic routing across models.

Core capabilities

Kong added MCP support in Gateway 3.12 in October 2025, as noted in its Gateway changelog. Its AI MCP Proxy plugin can expose REST APIs as MCP tools or sit in front of an MCP server. Access controls apply both when clients discover tools and when they invoke them. A companion OAuth2 plugin handles authentication for MCP traffic.

Where it fits

The main trade-offs are licensing and operational scope. Kong's documentation lists the MCP plugins as part of its AI Gateway Enterprise offering, and labels the OAuth2 plugin as a tech preview. If Kong is not already in your stack, deploying the full API gateway platform just for model traffic may be more than you need.

Best for: Organizations that already use Kong and want to manage AI traffic through their existing control plane.

3. Agent Router: Envoy-based routing for Kubernetes

Agent Router, formerly Envoy AI Gateway, is an Apache 2.0 project for managing access to hosted models, self-hosted inference and MCP servers. It provides an OpenAI-compatible API and is built around Envoy Gateway. The repository has moved to theagentrouter, but project documentation says the API resources, API group, CLI name and image paths remain unchanged.

Core capabilities

The project describes a two-tier pattern: one gateway handles shared authentication, routing and global limits, while another can manage traffic to self-hosted inference. It also offers a standalone CLI for local use, which makes it possible to try the API before deploying the Kubernetes components.

Where it fits

The trade-off is its platform focus. Teams already operating Envoy Gateway and Kubernetes have a clear path to evaluate it. For a small application that just needs a lightweight proxy, a simpler gateway may involve less setup. Its documentation and release notes are the best places to check the current status of specific providers and features.

Best for: Platform teams using Envoy Gateway or Kubernetes that want an open-source control plane for model and tool traffic.

4. Apache APISIX: Open-source AI plugins in an API gateway

Core capabilities

Apache APISIX is an Apache Software Foundation project licensed under Apache 2.0. Its open-source API gateway includes AI plugins for connecting to model providers, routing requests across instances, balancing traffic, retrying failures and limiting usage by tokens. The ai-proxy plugin supports documented providers and OpenAI-compatible APIs, while ai-proxy-multi adds multi-instance load balancing and fallback behavior. The ai-rate-limiting plugin applies token quotas.

APISIX also has an openapi-to-mcp plugin that exposes operations from an OpenAPI document as MCP tools. This is a useful contrast with Kong: APISIX's AI plugins are part of its open-source project, while Kong documents its MCP Proxy plugins as Enterprise features.

Where it fits

Because APISIX is a full API gateway, teams adopting it for AI traffic also take on its broader gateway configuration and operations. Its plugin model suits teams that want to manage API and model traffic together, with the AI capabilities available in the open-source project.

Best for: Platform teams that want an open-source API and AI gateway with multi-provider routing, token limits and MCP support.

5. LiteLLM: Broad provider support and a Python-first workflow

Core capabilities

LiteLLM is a common starting point for teams building with language models. It combines an MIT-licensed Python SDK with a self-hosted proxy that supports more than 100 providers, virtual keys, budgets, routing, fallbacks, guardrails and an MCP gateway. Semantic caching supports Qdrant, Valkey and Redis.

LiteLLM recommends semantic caching for single-shot prompts rather than multi-turn agent traffic, as explained in its documentation.

A paid enterprise license adds SCIM, audit logs and some guardrail integrations. Admin UI SSO is free for up to five users.

Trade-offs

Two considerations are worth a closer look. In an AWS EC2 test with 500 concurrent users over 60 seconds, Bifrost handled 424 requests per second with a P99 latency of 1.68 seconds, while LiteLLM handled 44.84 requests per second with a P99 latency of 90.72 seconds.

There was also a supply-chain incident. Malicious PyPI versions 1.82.7 and 1.82.8 were published on March 24, 2026. LiteLLM's security update says it believes the compromise originated from the Trivy dependency used in its CI/CD security-scanning workflow. The affected versions were removed. The incident involved a compromised package release rather than a vulnerability in LiteLLM's gateway code, and highlights the value of pinning dependencies and mirroring packages internally.

Best for: Python-focused teams with moderate traffic that value a broad provider ecosystem and can operate and secure a self-hosted service.

6. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway: Managed access for agents, tools and models

Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway is a managed AI gateway that provides a single entry point for agent traffic to tools, other agents and models. It can turn APIs, Lambda functions and existing services into MCP-compatible tools, and route inference requests across model providers.

Core capabilities

The gateway can combine APIs, functions, tools, agents and model providers behind one endpoint. It supports inbound and outbound authentication, credential exchange, semantic tool discovery and agent-to-agent traffic, with built-in observability and auditing.

Where it fits

As a fully managed AWS service, AgentCore Gateway may suit teams building on Amazon Bedrock that want to connect agents to existing tools without operating gateway infrastructure. Its AWS service scope and supported features should be checked against deployment and provider requirements.

Best for: Teams building on AWS that want managed access to agent tools, other agents and models through one gateway.

7. Azure API Management: AI gateway capabilities for models and agents

Azure API Management includes AI gateway capabilities for managing AI backends, models, agents and tools. It can manage language model APIs from Microsoft Foundry and other providers, remote MCP servers, A2A agent APIs, and self-hosted models.

Core capabilities

The AI gateway extends API Management's existing API gateway. It can authenticate and authorize access, load balance across AI endpoints, monitor and log interactions, manage token usage and quotas, expose REST APIs as MCP servers, and import A2A agent APIs. The unified model API is generally available in v2 tiers and available through early access for classic tiers via the AI Gateway Early release channel.

Where it fits

This option suits organizations already using Azure API Management that want to govern models, MCP servers and agent APIs through the same platform. Available capabilities vary by API Management tier, so check that the required features are included.

Best for: Teams that want to manage AI models, MCP servers and agent APIs through Azure API Management.

8. Cloudflare AI Gateway: Managed routing and observability

Cloudflare AI Gateway is a managed gateway for observing and controlling AI applications. It supports multiple model providers and provides analytics, request logging, caching, rate limiting, retries and model fallbacks.

Core capabilities

Applications can send requests through the gateway to supported providers. Model aliases and routing rules can choose providers and fallback models, while analytics and logs provide visibility into requests, token use, cost and errors.

Where it fits

Cloudflare AI Gateway is a managed service, so teams do not need to operate a gateway themselves. Its documented focus is model traffic and application-level controls; teams that need gateway-managed MCP servers or agent-to-agent routing should check whether they need an additional component.

Best for: Teams that want managed model routing, observability and traffic controls without running a gateway.

9. Vercel AI Gateway: Managed model access for apps and coding agents

Vercel AI Gateway provides a hosted API for accessing models across providers. It centralizes credentials, request logs, cost tracking, budgets, prompt caching and provider failover. Applications can use it from any cloud or language, and the documentation includes support for coding agents.

Core capabilities

The gateway can route requests across providers and fallback models, then record status, provider, latency, token usage, cost and routing attempts. It supports multiple modalities and tool calls when the selected model supports them.

Where it fits

Vercel AI Gateway can be used without running an application on Vercel, but teams need a Vercel account to create an API key and manage billing. Its documentation describes model access and tool calls, rather than a standalone MCP server gateway.

Best for: Teams that want hosted model access and provider failover for applications or coding agents.

Deployment and licensing compared

This table is a starting point, not a substitute for checking the current license and feature matrix. Some projects keep parts of their enterprise functionality outside the open-source gateway, while hosted gateways have their own service and usage terms.

Gateway License Where it runs Main trade-off
Bifrost Apache 2.0 core; Enterprise features are paid Self-hosted; private options in Enterprise Some governance and deployment features require Enterprise
Kong AI Gateway Apache 2.0 Kong Gateway; some AI plugins are paid Self-hosted, hybrid or Konnect Advanced AI features may require a license
Agent Router Apache 2.0 Kubernetes or standalone CLI Best suited to Envoy and Kubernetes stacks
Apache APISIX Apache 2.0 Self-hosted Broader API gateway to configure and operate
LiteLLM MIT core; some enterprise features are paid Self-hosted proxy Python-based operations and security upkeep
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway Managed AWS service AWS managed service AWS service scope and integrations
Azure API Management AI gateway Managed Azure service Azure API Management Capabilities vary by service tier
Cloudflare AI Gateway Managed service Cloudflare Managed service controls the data path
Vercel AI Gateway Managed service Hosted, usable from any cloud Requires a Vercel account for keys and billing

Which Agent Gateway Is Right for Your Team

If you are choosing a gateway for production, start with the constraints that matter most to your team. Bifrost provides multi-provider routing, agent workflows and private deployment options. Bifrost adds 11 µs of overhead at 5,000 RPS.

LiteLLM is a natural option for Python-centric teams. Kong fits organizations already running Kong, while Agent Router suits teams built around Envoy Gateway and Kubernetes. Apache APISIX adds AI capabilities to an open-source API gateway.

Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway and Azure API Management provide managed gateway options for teams using AWS and Azure, while Cloudflare and Vercel offer managed gateways as well. The best choice is the one that fits your existing platform and the amount of gateway operations your team is ready to own.

Frequently asked questions

What is an agent gateway?

An agent gateway sits between applications or agents and the models and tools they use. Depending on the project, it can provide a shared API, route requests, retry failures, apply usage limits and log traffic. Some gateways also manage MCP tools or agent-to-agent communication. Check the feature list because hosted services or enterprise controls may be separate.

How is an agent gateway different from an API gateway?

A traditional API gateway focuses on routing and authentication for general API traffic. An agent gateway can add features for model requests and agent tools, such as provider routing, token-based limits, model fallbacks, MCP access controls and usage reporting. Some API gateways now offer AI plugins as well, so the distinction depends on the product.

Should we self-host or use a managed gateway?

Self-hosting gives your team more control over prompts, keys and logs, but also means operating the service. A managed gateway can be quicker to adopt, though traffic passes through the vendor's network. The right choice depends on your security requirements and the operational support available to your team.

Do LLM gateways support MCP?

MCP support varies. Bifrost has a native MCP gateway, Kong offers AI MCP Proxy plugins, Agent Router handles AI and MCP traffic, Apache APISIX provides an openapi-to-mcp plugin, LiteLLM includes MCP support in its proxy, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway connects agents to MCP-compatible tools, and Azure API Management can manage MCP servers. Compare authentication and tool-level permissions rather than treating support as a yes-or-no feature.

How much latency does an LLM gateway add?

The answer depends on the gateway, workload and enabled features. Bifrost adds about 11 microseconds of overhead at 5,000 requests per second on a single t3.xlarge. That is small next to the time many models take to respond, but added latency can matter when an agent makes a long sequence of calls.

Can we move off LiteLLM without rewriting code?

Often, yes. Both products expose OpenAI-compatible APIs, and Bifrost provides drop-in adapters for the LiteLLM SDK. Teams using the LiteLLM proxy can also migrate models, keys, teams and users. See the LiteLLM migration guide for the process and its details.

Can an LLM gateway govern employees using ChatGPT or Claude desktop apps?

Only when that traffic passes through the gateway. A standard gateway typically sees requests that developers have configured to use it. Bifrost Edge is designed to route traffic from desktop apps, browsers and coding agents through Bifrost so gateway policies can apply.

Is Bifrost open source, and what does the Enterprise tier add?

Bifrost's core is open source under Apache 2.0 and can be self-hosted for free. The Enterprise tier adds high availability, identity-based governance, guardrail and vault integrations, signed audit logs, and in-VPC or air-gapped deployment. It includes a 14-day free trial. Bifrost Edge requires an Enterprise gateway and is priced per endpoint.

Conclusion

There is no single gateway that is right for every stack. Choose based on the providers you use, how you plan to deploy, and whether you want a dedicated model proxy, agent and tool controls, or AI features inside an existing API platform. Check each gateway's feature boundaries, and test the options with your own workload before committing. If Bifrost is on your shortlist, its documentation and demo cover its deployment and Enterprise options.

Resources:

  • Bifrost Docs: https://docs.getbifrost.ai
  • Bifrost CLI: npx -y @maximhq/bifrost-cli

articles.title: The Art of the Canary in the Age of AI
articles.description: Companion repository: copyleftdev/canary-article — full experiment, source code, run artifacts,...
articles.body_html:
Companion repository: copyleftdev/canary-article — full experiment, source code, run artifacts, and evidence explorer. All 30 main-attempt results are inspectable.

The first completed pilot run produced exactly the signal we had asked for:

CANARY:fd11c73f1ba333de

Then the agent explained that it couldn't access the project files or run checks. Our container was missing an execution helper, codex-code-mode-host. The requested feature had not been implemented.

The canary was present. The work could not proceed.

That was an infrastructure failure in our pilot, not a discovered booking bug or a result from the main experiment. The distinction became the first useful lesson of the project: a visible signal needs a precise meaning.

We preserved the failed pilot, documented the runtime defect, and started a replacement cohort after fixing it. You can inspect the original response, independent evaluation, and amendment.

The question behind the experiment survived: what does an instruction canary actually tell us about an AI coding agent's work?

A small signal with a long history

Mining canaries responded to dangerous gases before their human handlers did. One detail makes that history more interesting than the familiar metaphor: the Science Museum holds a canary cage equipped with an oxygen cylinder. Its design allowed a poisoned bird to be enclosed and given oxygen. Detection was connected to a response. Science Museum collection

Software borrowed the canary metaphor. A deployment canary exposes a limited population to a change and evaluates it against a control before a wider rollout. Google's SRE workbook describes both the rollout and the evaluation needed to make that useful. Canarying Releases

An instruction canary uses a different mechanism. We place a small requirement in project instructions and look for its observable effect: perhaps a recognizable word at the start of the agent's response.

That output proves something narrow: the response satisfied that particular requirement. Establishing a relationship to other behavior takes additional evidence.

This technique already has implementations. Context Canary displays a bird associated with a response marker and supports checkpoints distributed through instructions. Its documentation also explains that a missing marker does not prove context loss. Our contribution is a reproducible experiment that puts the marker beside independent checks of the resulting code.

Give the canary one clear job

Here is the instruction used in our marker condition, with an example token:

The first nonempty line of your final response must be exactly
CANARY:0123456789abcdef, with no other characters on that line.
Put all other text on subsequent lines.

It belongs in a project instruction file supported by the chosen coding tool. For Codex, AGENTS.md participates in a documented discovery chain with project and global scopes. Verify the applicable location and overrides for your tool; an instruction sitting on disk is not automatically evidence that it reached the model. Codex instruction discovery

Our runner generates a different token for every marker run. It puts that instruction in AGENTS.md, without repeating the token in the task prompt. The scorer checks the terminal final response, excluding tool output and intermediate messages.

We distinguish exact matches, malformed occurrences, absent tokens, and unobserved final responses. A timeout with no final response is not the same observation as a response that omitted its marker.

We also keep four questions separate:

  • What evidence shows that the instructions were loaded?
  • Did the final response satisfy the marker instruction?
  • Did the resulting code pass the specified behavioral checks?
  • Was the requested feature actually completed?

Instruction context and enforcement are different mechanisms. Anthropic makes that distinction explicitly in its memory documentation, which also describes loading diagnostics and hooks. How Claude remembers your project

Build something worth checking

Our experimental subject is a small Python booking module with two meeting rooms. It has no database, web server, or current-time dependency. That keeps the work small enough to inspect while giving mistakes a concrete meaning.

Its contract includes three important rules: reservations for the same room must not overlap; timestamps must carry an explicit offset and be normalized to UTC; rejected operations must leave existing bookings unchanged.

Adjacent reservations are allowed. Different rooms may be booked at the same time. These details are written down before the agent starts, because hidden checks should exercise a published contract rather than introduce surprise requirements.

Each run starts from the same working baseline and gets one task:

  1. Add rescheduling while preserving a booking's identity and room.
  2. Return the rooms available during a requested interval.
  3. Add a batch of reservations atomically, so one invalid member prevents the entire batch from being saved.

The fixture contract defines the API and edge cases. The tasks are independent; a later task does not inherit an earlier agent's implementation.

Test the measuring equipment

Before measuring agents, we calibrated the evaluator with 16 cases. They include correct implementations, deliberately broken overlap and timestamp handling, partial batch writes, missing features, import failures, and an import that hangs.

All 16 met their calibration expectations. That means the evaluator recognized the expected outcomes; it does not mean the deliberately broken programs passed the booking checks. For the hanging import, the expected outcome was a timeout with unevaluable behavior and verified container cleanup. These cases are test equipment validation, not model runs. Calibration record

The agent can see public examples. Evaluator-owned checks and reference implementations remain outside its container. After the agent stops, the saved submission runs in a separate evaluation container without network access or credentials.

This arrangement also keeps the agent's claim that tests passed separate from the evaluator's evidence. A feature can be missing even while the original baseline still passes its existing-operation checks—as our failed runtime pilot demonstrated.

After repairing that runtime, we completed six replacement pilot runs: one marker and one no-marker run for each task. All six passed their independent rule and feature checks; all three marker responses matched exactly. Those pilots checked that the procedure worked. They remain outside the main dataset. Replacement pilot report

Freeze the comparison before reading the result

The main plan contains 30 attempts: three tasks, two conditions, and five repetitions. Fifteen runs receive the marker instruction. The other fifteen receive the same project rules without it.

We randomize task/repetition blocks and the order of the two conditions within each block. Sessions and workspaces start fresh. This study uses Codex CLI 0.166.0, the gpt-6-astra model alias, high reasoning effort, and a 240-second limit per attempt. The saved plan records those settings, the runtime image, source hashes, and execution order. The underlying provider backend revision is unavailable, which limits exact model reproducibility.

We froze the plan before main collection. Failed attempts remain in the ledger rather than being silently retried or replaced. This is a local audit trail, not a public preregistration.

Thirty attempts are a small exploratory case study. Repeated calls to the same model do not establish independent samples, and hundreds of test assertions do not turn one agent run into hundreds of observations. Full protocol

The result was uniformly green

All 30 main attempts completed. Every submission built and passed both its feature-acceptance and project-rule checks. There were no main-study timeouts, interrupted attempts, missing final responses, or unevaluable results.

Task No marker: feature and rule checks passed With marker: feature and rule checks passed Exact markers
Rescheduling 5/5 5/5 5/5
Availability 5/5 5/5 5/5
Atomic batch booking 5/5 5/5 5/5

Among the fifteen marker-enabled runs, the table was equally simple:

Marker instruction Rule checks passed Rule checks failed
Exact match 15 0
Noncompliant marker 0 0

The fifteen no-marker controls do not belong in that second table. Their feature and rule outcomes remain in the first one. None of the marker runs were excluded for unavailable evidence. Complete main-study report

For a representative example, reschedule-01-B returned its exact marker and passed the independent checks. All fifteen marker-enabled runs shared that overall outcome.

This supports a narrow observation: the marker format was followed in every marker-enabled run in this setup. It does not establish the marker's value as a warning signal. We saw neither a marker omission nor a checked rule failure, so we cannot compare failure rates between compliant and noncompliant responses. The fraction of failures accompanied by a warning is undefined because there were no observed failures.

These were short edits to a working baseline that already supplied timestamp normalization and conflict-checking helpers. We did not test long-session drift or large architectural changes. Automatic instruction-loading diagnostics were unavailable, although pilot transcripts recorded explicit reads of AGENTS.md. We kept the fixed tasks and sample rather than increasing difficulty until a disagreement appeared. A study of warning lead time would need a different, longitudinal design.

Make the evidence easy to inspect

The companion project, Canary Lab, produces a standalone HTML report and machine-readable JSON. Each planned run stays visible. Marker status, feature completion, rule checks, and missing evidence have separate fields. The evidence explorer lets you filter by task or condition and expand a run's instructions, prompt, final response, code diff, and evaluation.

Saved submissions can be evaluated again without another model call. That makes the project useful beyond the article: readers can investigate a surprising result or adapt the contract to their own project. The run guide covers setup, calibration, pilots, collection, and replay.

What this study can and cannot tell you

This experiment produced a uniform-green result: 30/30 passed, 15/15 markers matched. That supports a narrow claim — the canary format is followable — but it invites the right challenges. Here are the ones I expect, and what the evidence actually says.

"You only tested short, isolated tasks." Correct. Each run is a fresh session with a single edit against a working baseline that already provides timestamp normalization and overlap helpers. Long-session drift, multi-turn state decay, and context-window pressure are not tested. The study would need a different, longitudinal design to measure those.

"You tested on a model that is too good to fail." Possible. We used gpt-6-astra with high reasoning effort. A weaker model might omit the marker more often — which is exactly where the canary DIAGNOSTIC value would appear. The uniform-green result means either the task was too easy or the model was too reliable. Both are genuine limitations, and the protocol is explicit about them.

"The canary proves nothing about code correctness." It does not. We keep four questions separate on purpose: instruction loading, marker compliance, behavioral checks, and feature completion. A present canary does not mean the feature was built correctly. An absent one means something is wrong upstream — but we had zero absent markers, so we cannot demonstrate that link.

"AGENTS.md might not have been loaded." For Codex, AGENTS.md participates in a documented discovery chain. Pilot transcripts recorded explicit reads of the file. Automatic loading diagnostics were not available at the time, so we cannot rule out a silent skip. A tool that exposes loading evidence would strengthen this.

"Correlation is not causation — even if a marker omission preceded a failure, that would not prove the omission caused it." True. A missing canary and a booking-rule failure could both be downstream of the same root cause (context loss, instruction collision, timeout). The canary is a diagnostic signal, not a causal proof. Its value is in making invisible failures visible so you can investigate.

"30 runs is not a study." It is a small exploratory case study. The n=30 does not establish independent samples (same model, same session structure), and 15 marker vs 15 control runs provide zero failures to correlate against. The companion project is built so anyone can run it with more models, harder tasks, or longer sessions and produce new evidence.

"The canary instruction itself could influence the agent's behavior." It could. The marker instruction occupies tokens in context. It might compete with the task instructions for attention. We did not measure an attention-budget effect. A study isolating that would need a control condition with an equal-length neutral instruction.

These are not weaknesses to hide behind caveats. They are the limits of what a 30-run single-model experiment can claim. The project is public precisely so someone else can push past these limits — with more models, longer sessions, harder tasks, and a result that breaks the streak.

What to do with an instruction canary in a real project

Start with one cheap, unambiguous marker and a specific question about instruction handling. Confirm how your tool loads it. Keep the marker easy to recognize and avoid treating a general “rules followed” statement as evidence for every rule.

Pair it with a check of the behavior you care about. If the concern is overlapping reservations, exercise overlapping reservations. If a requirement must hold at a particular tool boundary, consider an appropriate enforcement mechanism there.

Decide what an omission should prompt. Inspect loading diagnostics, check for conflicting instructions, re-establish the relevant requirement, and run its independent check. These are proposed engineering practices; this experiment does not compare recovery strategies or rank canary designs.

The craft is in matching a small signal to a question it can help answer—and keeping the evidence that answers the larger questions beside it.

articles.title: I store face embeddings in a hand-rolled write-ahead log, and it works great
articles.description: A few months ago I started building FaceMark, an attendance system that recognizes students' faces. A...
articles.body_html:
A few months ago I started building FaceMark, an attendance system that recognizes students' faces. A NestJS API handles auth, courses and attendance records, and a small FastAPI service runs DeepFace/TensorFlow to turn face photos into 512-dimensional embedding vectors and match them.

The AI service needs to persist those embeddings. My first version did what every tutorial does: a Python dictionary, pickled to a file.

It worked, right up until I thought about it for five minutes:

  • Every save rewrote the entire file. One crash mid-write and I lose every registered face.
  • No integrity checks. A corrupt byte somewhere means pickle.load explodes and I find out at 8 AM when a classroom full of students is waiting.
  • No deletes. Removing a student meant loading everything, popping a key, and rewriting everything.

I could have reached for SQLite, Redis, or a vector database. For the actual scale of this problem (a few thousand embeddings, writes only when a new student registers) all of them felt like operating a forklift to move a bookshelf. What I wanted was exactly the thing from Chapter 3 of Designing Data-Intensive Applications: an append-only log with an in-memory index, the Bitcask model. So I built it. It's about 200 lines of Python and it's been boringly reliable ever since.

The record format

Every record in the log is:

[CRC32: 4B][Timestamp: 8B][Tombstone: 1B][KeyLen: 2B][ValLen: 4B][Key][Value]

19 bytes of header, then the raw key and value. Keys are student IDs, values are JSON-encoded embedding vectors.

Writes are the simplest possible thing: seek to the end of the file, append the record, fsync, and update two in-memory structures — a keydir mapping each key to its (offset, size, timestamp) in the file, and a hot cache holding the actual vectors:

self._file.seek(0, os.SEEK_END)
offset = self._file.tell()
self._file.write(record)
self._file.flush()
os.fsync(self._file.fileno())

self._keydir[key] = (offset, len(record), ts)
self._cache[key] = embedding

No seeking, no in-place updates, no locks to reason about. The file only ever grows.

Why the CRC32 earns its 4 bytes

The header starts with a CRC32 checksum over the rest of the record. On startup the engine scans the log sequentially and rebuilds the keydir and cache. If it hits a truncated record (the classic "process died mid-write" case) it stops there and discards the tail. If a record's CRC doesn't match, it logs the offset and skips it:

expected_crc = zlib.crc32(raw_header_payload + raw_payload) & 0xffffffff
if crc != expected_crc:
    print(f"[DDIA-WAL] Error: CRC mismatch at offset {offset}")
    corrupt_records += 1
    continue

This is the whole point of the exercise: a crash can cost me at most the tail of the file, never the whole store, and I always know exactly which record was lost. With the pickle file, the answer to "how much did I just lose?" was "yes."

Deletes are just more appends

You can't erase bytes from an append-only log, so deletes append a tombstone record — same format, tombstone flag set, empty value. During recovery, a tombstone removes the key from the index:

if tombstone == 1:
    self._keydir.pop(key, None)
    self._cache.pop(key, None)

Compaction keeps the file honest

Appending forever means superseded records pile up: every re-registered face and every tombstone is dead weight. Compaction writes only the currently-live records to a temporary file, then atomically renames it over the old log:

self._file.close()
os.replace(compact_path, self.wal_path)
self._file = open(self.wal_path, "a+b")
self._recover()

os.replace is atomic on both POSIX and Windows, so a crash during compaction leaves either the old file or the new one fully intact — never a half-written mix.

Reads and the actual workload

Face recognition needs every embedding to compare a camera frame against, so all_embeddings() just returns the in-memory cache — the comparison loop never touches disk at all. Single-key get checks the cache first, falls back to a keydir lookup, one seek and one read.

This is the part where the "just use a database" objection is fair, so let me be honest about the tradeoffs:

  • Everything lives in RAM. Fine for thousands of 512-float vectors, wrong for millions.
  • Single writer. There is no concurrency control because my workload has exactly one writer.
  • fsync on every write is slow. My writes happen a few times per day, so I happily pay milliseconds for durability.
  • Similarity search is brute-force linear scan. At this scale numpy does it faster than I can blink. When it stops being fast, that's a good problem to have, and the WAL still works as the persistence layer under a proper index.

The migration escape hatch

One detail I'm glad I added: on first run, if no WAL exists but the old pickle file does, the engine converts every record into WAL format before opening the store. Existing deployments upgrade themselves with zero drama.

What I got out of it

Building this taught me more about storage than a month of reading would have. Record framing, checksums, tombstones, atomic rename, crash recovery — these stopped being vocabulary and became code I had to get right. The full implementation is in the FaceMark repo (ai-service/wal_engine.py) if you want to pick it apart: https://github.com/ZiadtahaM/FaceMark

If you're storing something small, written rarely, and read constantly, and you're about to spin up Redis for it, maybe spend an afternoon with DDIA chapter 3 first.

articles.title: One Script, Four Documents
articles.description: The rules were already knowable, so I didn't put a model in the pipeline.  A video course may begin...
articles.body_html:
The rules were already knowable, so I didn't put a model in the pipeline.

A video course may begin with one master script, but the people producing it rarely need the same document. The presenter needs clean narration for a teleprompter. The screencast recorder needs actions, commands, visual cues, and voiceover. The motion designer needs animation instructions. The producer needs an overview of the videos, their components, and approximate runtimes.

Maintaining those as four independent documents creates a familiar problem. The moment the script changes, someone has to remember every downstream copy. A corrected line of narration might reach the presenter but not the producer. A revised demonstration might appear in the recording instructions but not the production plan. The documents are all plausible, yet they no longer describe the same course.

I've run into versions of this coordination problem for years, building curriculum at MongoDB University and working with developers through Cisco DevNet, and I wanted to try something different: treat the master production script as structured source material, validate it, and generate the role-specific documents deterministically. Instead of asking people to reconcile several copies, make the copies products of the same source.

I built the experiment around a fictional course, Understanding APIs: A Winery's Digital Cellar. The winery setting was a convenient way to make an API course approachable, and I enjoy projects where the example has a little personality. But the winery API isn't the real experiment. The production workflow is. I wanted something small enough to understand end to end, yet realistic enough to expose the places where documents drift apart.

The rules were already knowable

The hard part isn't generating text. It's keeping the outputs consistent with the source.

A language model could read a script and draft separate production documents. That introduces an interpretive step, and for this workflow there is nothing to interpret. A [SCREENCAST] section belongs in the screencast document. An [ONSET] section belongs in the presenter document. An [ACTION] is a production instruction and a [VOICEOVER] is spoken narration. The generator does not need to decide what the author meant each time it runs, because the author already said so in the markup.

So the project uses a small, explicit grammar. The master script organizes content by stage and video, with tagged production sections and annotations inside them. Those tags are instructions to a parser, not prompts asking a model to infer structure.

Figure 1. The master script organizes content by stage and video, with tagged production sections inside each.

Worth being clear about what this is and isn't an argument for. I used an AI coding agent heavily while building this thing. What I didn't do was leave one in the pipeline. Those are different decisions, and conflating them is how you end up with an interpretive layer in a transformation whose rules you could have written down. Use a model where the rules aren't knowable. Where they are, write the rules.

A parser turns the source into a structured intermediate representation. Validation checks that sections are well formed and that the expected course structure is present. Only then does the generator prepare outputs.

Figure 2. The pipeline. Validation sits between parsing and any Drive write, so a malformed source produces diagnostics instead of documents.

The separation matters. Parsing establishes what the document says structurally. Validation decides whether it is safe to proceed. Estimation calculates values under stated assumptions. Rendering turns validated data into documents for different readers. None of those steps needs to invent missing content.

One source, different readers

The example course contains two stages, six videos, and thirteen production sections: six ONSET, three MOTION, four SCREENCAST. Some videos combine a presenter introduction with a screencast. Others use motion graphics, or return to the presenter after a demonstration.

That last case is the useful one for testing. "Handling Errors," the second video of stage two, runs ONSET → MOTION → SCREENCAST → ONSET, which means a single video contains two distinct presenter segments separated by other production material. The generated ONSET document identifies them as Part 1 of 2 and Part 2 of 2 rather than running them together as though the presenter never left.

The ONSET document carries narration and pause cues without the screencast directions. The SCREENCAST document preserves the sequence of actions, highlights, and voiceover, including example API requests and JSON responses. The MOTION document serves the animation role. The Production Summary provides counts, estimates, and warnings across the course.

Figure 3. Each run creates a new folder: four role-specific documents plus the manifest that records how they were made.

Figure 4. The same source, two readers. The presenter gets narration and pause cues. The screencast producer gets actions, examples, and voiceover.

These aren't four independently authored interpretations of the script. They are four views of the same validated structure. An editor changes the master document and runs generation again, and the previous output set remains a snapshot of the earlier run.

A validation gate before any Drive writes

The most important feature may be what happens when the source is wrong.

The project includes deliberately malformed script fixtures: missing closing tags, unexpected closing tags, nested production sections, unknown annotations. The parser returns diagnostics with source locations rather than trying to repair the document silently. Validation runs before output creation, so a malformed source blocks generation and the workflow never produces a polished-looking set of documents from a broken script.

That's a modest rule. It's also the difference between automation that produces files and automation that enforces a contract.

It also creates a useful exercise: introduce an error into a copy of the master script, read the diagnostic, confirm that generation is blocked, correct the source, run validation again. The failure is part of the lesson rather than something to hide from the learner.

A polished success path shows what a tool can do. A controlled failure shows what the system actually guarantees, where the boundary sits, and how to recover. I've written before about tests that cannot fail, and a generation step with no negative control has the same problem: it certifies nothing, confidently.

Estimation is not observation

The fourth document adds a production estimate. The estimator counts spoken words from ONSET narration and VOICEOVER blocks, excluding directions such as ACTION, VISUAL, and HIGHLIGHT. At the default assumption of 140 words per minute, it calculates narration duration per video, and videos over a configurable threshold get a warning.

That sounds straightforward until the numbers acquire an undeserved aura of precision. A word count is an observed property of the script under a counting rule. A duration is a calculation from an assumed speaking rate. Actual recording time includes pauses, interactions, retakes, animation, and editing choices the model doesn't capture.

So the Production Summary states its rules rather than describing them. The counting rule, verbatim from the generated document:

A word is a whitespace-separated token with at least one letter or digit. Contractions, hyphenated terms, numbers, and URLs or code in narration each count as one word, as written.

It also states its rounding policy: durations round to the nearest second for display, while totals and the threshold check use unrounded values, so a displayed value can sit exactly at the threshold and the displayed per-video figures may not add up precisely to the total.

And where an assumption has no evidence behind it, it says so. The screencast allowance is configurable and currently set to zero seconds per section, which makes every figure a narration-only estimate. The document is explicit that this "isn't a claim that screen actions take no time; no evidence-based figure has been set." I find that distinction worth more than a plausible guess would be.

Figure 5. The Production Summary: counted words, estimated duration, and threshold status per video, with the assumptions stated underneath.

In the current live run, the six videos contain 1,978 counted spoken words and an estimated 14 minutes 8 seconds of narration at 140 words per minute. One video trips the three-minute warning: "Handling Errors," at 664 words and 4 minutes 45 seconds. The hardest video to parse correctly turns out to be the one the estimator flags as too long, which is a coincidence I enjoyed more than I should have.

An earlier run counted 1,980 words. An editorial revision reduced the count by two, which is exactly the kind of drift the manifest exists to make legible.

The estimator also annotates counts that deserve suspicion. Four of the six videos carry notes like "includes 2 URL, path, or code tokens that may take longer to narrate," because a URL read aloud is one word by the counting rule and considerably more than one word of speech.

The point isn't that 14 minutes 8 seconds will be the final course runtime. It's that the estimate is reproducible, its assumptions are visible, and a change to it can be explained.

The manifest is part of the deliverable

Every generation run creates a new output folder rather than overwriting an earlier set. Alongside the four Google Docs, a JSON manifest records the source document reference and the hash of its text, the parser and estimator versions and their hashes, the configuration, output references, counts, and warnings.
